questions.stem: Which function has a removable discontinuity at x = 3?
questions.solution: The function f(x) has a removable discontinuity at x = 3 because the factor (x - 3) can be cancelled out, making it continuous after simplification. The other options either have vertical asymptotes (B), are continuous at x = 3 (C), or do not have a hole at x = 3 (D).
questions.explanation: Removable discontinuities occur when the function is undefined due to a removable factor, such as a cancelled out denominator.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing B because it has a similar structure but does not cancel out, resulting in a vertical asymptote.

questions.stem: What type of discontinuity does f(x) = 1/x have at x = 0?
questions.solution: The function f(x) has an infinite discontinuity at x = 0 because the limit approaches infinity as x approaches 0 from both sides. There is no way to remove the discontinuity.
questions.explanation: Infinite discontinuities occur when the limit of a function approaches infinity or negative infinity at a specific point.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing A, thinking that removing the factor would make it continuous, but x cannot be 0.

questions.stem: Which function has a jump discontinuity at x = 2?
questions.solution: The function g(x) has a jump discontinuity at x = 2 because the limit from the left (g(2-) = 0) is different from the limit from the right (g(2+) = 2). The other options are continuous or have removable discontinuities.
questions.explanation: Jump discontinuities occur when the function's value changes abruptly at a point without approaching infinity.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing B, which has a removable discontinuity rather than a jump.

questions.stem: What type of discontinuity does f(x) = 1/(x - 1)^2 have at x = 1?
questions.solution: The function f(x) has an infinite discontinuity at x = 1 because the limit approaches infinity as x approaches 1. There is no way to remove the discontinuity.
questions.explanation: Infinite discontinuities occur when the limit of a function approaches infinity or negative infinity at a specific point.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing A, thinking that removing the factor would make it continuous, but x cannot be 1.

questions.stem: Which function has a removable discontinuity at x = -2?
questions.solution: The function g(x) has a removable discontinuity at x = -2 because the factor (x + 2) can be cancelled out, making it continuous after simplification. The other options are either continuous or have infinite discontinuities.
questions.explanation: Removable discontinuities occur when the function is undefined due to a removable factor, such as a cancelled out denominator.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing B because it has no discontinuity at x = -2.

questions.stem: What type of discontinuity does f(x) = [x] have at x = 1?
questions.solution: The function f(x) = [x], the greatest integer function, has a jump discontinuity at x = 1 because the value of the function changes from 0 to 1 as x increases past 1. The other options do not describe this type of behavior.
questions.explanation: Jump discontinuities occur when the function's value changes abruptly at a point without approaching infinity.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing A, thinking that [x] is continuous, but it actually has jumps at integer values.

questions.stem: Which of the following functions has no discontinuities?
questions.solution: The function h(x) = 3x - 6 is continuous for all real numbers because it is a linear function with no undefined points or infinite limits.
questions.explanation: Continuous functions have no breaks, jumps, or asymptotes in their graphs; they can be drawn without lifting the pencil.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing A, which has a removable discontinuity at x = 0.
